steps.text: Part 3 of 4: Forks: how to see them, set them up and stop them. This part covers . Each part is short on purpose: finish one, play a game or take a break, and come back.

**Royal and discovered forks.** When the king is a target, the check must be answered first, so the other target cannot simply move away. [I] That makes a check fork the cleanest kind; each board below is checked, the generalisation is my inference. A discovered attack adds a free second threat: a piece moves with a threat of its own and uncovers a line behind it.

steps.caption: A royal fork: the king is one target. White to move.

line.say: The knight checks the king on c7 and attacks the rook on e3.
The king must move; the rook cannot.
The knight takes the rook.
The bishop retakes: the rook was guarded.
The queen retakes the bishop. The rook was guarded, but the trade still wins a rook and a bishop for a knight.

claims.statement: The knight attacks the king on c7.
The knight attacks the rook on e3.
Along the engine line the knight move nets material.

steps.caption: A discovered fork: a bishop move that uncovers a rook. White to move.

line.say: The bishop checks the king and attacks the rook on a2, and it uncovers the rook on h1.
The king steps aside.
The rook takes the queen.

claims.statement: After the bishop moves, the rook on h1 attacks the queen on e1.
The bishop attacks the king on g8.
The bishop attacks the rook on a2.
Along the engine line the bishop move wins material.

steps.text: **Stopping a fork against you.** Before you move, list the opponent's checks, captures and threats that your move allows. Heisman calls skipping this *Hope Chess* [S]; he also pairs it with finding the threat, then preventing it [S]. For forks, look for squares an enemy knight can reach that touch two of your pieces. Aagaard (as a reviewer of his book reports it) says serious errors often begin when a key candidate is overlooked [S].

steps.caption: White's rook is not attacked, but White considers retreating it to e1. Which squares give a black knight check, and what else does f3 hit?

line.say: The rook retreats to the back rank.
The knight jumps to f3: a check on the king that also attacks the rook.
The king steps aside.
The knight takes the rook.

claims.statement: The knight attacks the king on h2.
The knight attacks the rook on e1.
Along the engine line the retreat loses material.

steps.text: Kg3 keeps the balance (about +0.6 at depth 18 [V]); the rook retreat is far worse. Before any quiet move, list the squares from which an enemy knight gives check, and ask what else each one touches.

**Mixed test.** Eight unlabelled positions: some forks, some other tactics, some where no fork works. Aim for 6 of 8; that threshold is our choice, not a research finding. Two of the eight are yes/no, so guessing alone scores about one. If you miss a pin or a skewer, that is another lesson, not a fork failure. Note which search order you used.

steps.prompt: Which kind of piece did you miss most often in the mixed test? Eight positions are too few to test the knight idea, so treat this as a note, not a result. Did the order you searched in make a difference?

fields.label: The piece I missed most:
options: it was a pin or skewer, not a fork

steps.text: **Two real games.** Byrne v Fischer, New York 1956, and Anderssen v Dufresne, Berlin, usually dated 1852 (the date and status of that game are disputed [S, reviewer's note; not checked here]). Each has a fork-shaped move at a decision point. Predict first: does it win material, and what does the other side hold in reserve? The full games have their own lessons.

steps.caption: Byrne v Fischer, New York 1956: White to move at move 14. Black has just taken a pawn on e4. Predict first, then step through.

line.say: The bishop forks the queen and the rook. But the rook is guarded twice, by the bishop on g7 and the king, so taking it wins only the exchange.
The queen moves and attacks with it, so White has no time to take the rook for free.
White develops and eyes f7, though that pawn is defended.
The knight takes a pawn and attacks the rook on d1: Black's own fork.
White attacks the queen again with the bishop.

claims.statement: The bishop on e7 attacks the queen on d8.
The bishop on e7 attacks the rook on f8.
The queen on b6 and the bishop on g7 both attack the pawn on d4.
The bishop on c4 attacks the pawn on f7.
The knight on c3 attacks the rook on d1.
The bishop on c5 attacks the queen on b6.
Along the engine line the bishop move nets no material.

steps.text: **A fork that wins the exchange can lose the game if the other side gets there first.** After the bishop fork the engine rates the position about 2.9 pawns better for Black at depth 16 [V]. Fischer won this game [R].

steps.prompt: Black can take the knight with the g-pawn. Does White still have something? Decide, then step through the line.

steps.caption: Anderssen v Dufresne, Berlin, usually dated 1852: the fork that can be captured. White to move.

line.say: The knight checks the king on e8 and attacks the queen on h5.
The pawn on g7 takes the knight. White has given up a piece.
White recaptures with the pawn.
Black attacks along the g-file.

claims.statement: The knight attacks the queen on h5.
The pawn on g7 attacks the knight on f6.
Along the engine line the knight jump nets no material.
The knight jump is worse than the engine's best move at depth 16, so it is a sacrifice, not a plain fork.

steps.text: **The engine's view.** At depth 16 the engine prefers a quieter move (about +5.6) but still rates the sacrifice about +1.0 for White [V]. The move is sound but not the best: a different kind of move, not a mistake.

steps.prompt: [H] A guess, not a finding: Anderssen may have judged that the open lines were worth more than the knight he gave up. A fork that loses the forker can still be right if something more is behind it. What would you want to see on the board before sacrificing the forker?

fields.label: What I would want to see:

steps.text: **Remember.** When the king is one target, the check must be answered, so the other piece cannot escape. Before a quiet move, list the squares where an enemy knight could check and ask what else it would hit. A fork also fails if the other side gets there first.
